title: Making introductions: connecting two people who should meet
description: A good introduction is a small gift: it hands two people a reason to talk and a thread to pull. Done well, it takes thirty seconds and can start friendships, collaborations and occasionally whole chapters of a life.

body.heading: Give them a thread, not just names
paragraphs: “Sam, this is Priya” is information, not an introduction. Add the thread: “Priya, this is Sam — he is restoring a canal boat, and you told me last week you want to learn to sail.” Now the first question asks itself, and neither person has to perform the awkward excavation of finding common ground.
One true, specific detail about each person is enough. Choose something they are happy to have shared — a project, a place, an enthusiasm — never something private, medical, financial or gossipy.

body.heading: Ask both sides first
paragraphs: Before connecting two people by message or email, check with each of them separately. A short note — “I know someone restoring a boat who would love your sailing stories; may I introduce you?” — protects everyone's privacy and turns the introduction into an invitation rather than an ambush.
If either person declines, accept it completely and without reporting back the refusal in detail. The introducer's job is to open doors, not to push people through them.

body.heading: Stay for the first minute, then leave
paragraphs: In person, remain for the first exchange or two, topping up the thread if it frays: “Sam, Priya's first sailing trip was in a storm — ask her about it.” Once the conversation is carrying its own weight, drift away and let it belong to them.

And if nothing catches? That is fine too. Not every introduction becomes a friendship, and a introducer who never takes that personally will keep making them — which is how networks, and neighbourhoods, actually grow.

takeaway: Introduce people with a specific shared thread, ask both sides first, stay for the first minute, then let the connection belong to them.
